UnitStatement: The chapter surveys AI agent architectures, LLM reliability, formal methods, professional engineering regulation, and epistemic frameworks as domains converging in Chirality.
The literature review frames the central gap as the absence of architecturally enforced governance for LLM-based agent systems in regulated professional practice.
The literature review supports thesis novelty by showing that the Chapter 1 contributions address gaps not filled by existing work.
Chirality derives its epistemic architecture from provenance theory and hallucination research.
Chirality derives its invariant system from formal methods.
Chirality derives its regulatory mapping from professional practice standards.
Chirality derives its agent type hierarchy from multi-agent systems research.
LLM-based autonomous agent research since 2022 has focused on agent capabilities such as reasoning, planning, tool use, delegation, and collaboration.
Section 2.1 surveys agent patterns, multi-agent frameworks, and alignment techniques to identify Chirality's governance gap.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves large language model performance on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning by eliciting intermediate reasoning steps.
Chain-of-thought capability emerges as a function of model scale and requires only few-shot in-context examples.
Chirality uses chain-of-thought as the reasoning mode for agents operating within the ANALYST and AUDITOR tiers.
Chirality layers structural constraints over chain-of-thought because chain-of-thought alone does not provide governance controls.
ReAct interleaves language-model reasoning traces with action calls against external tools or environments.
ReAct grounds reasoning in retrieved evidence, reducing hallucination and error propagation relative to pure chain-of-thought in cited evaluations.
ReAct influenced Chirality's deterministic tool interface in which agents reason about invocations, invoke tools, and receive structured results.
The ReAct paper does not specify constraints on tool invocations, permissible side effects, or authority boundaries over the action space.
Toolformer shows that models can learn when and how to call a fixed set of external APIs in a self-supervised manner.
Toolformer is relevant to Chirality's TOOLMAKER subsystem because Chirality provides deterministic and auditable tool implementations.
Toolformer treats tool invocation as a capability to maximize without defining read-only versus write-capable tool boundaries.
Toolformer does not specify authority conditions under which write operations are permissible.
AutoGen introduced conversable agents and conversation programming for composing LLM applications from autonomous or human-proxy agents.
AutoGen role separation is a precursor to Chirality's tiered authority model but assigns roles for specialization rather than governance.
AutoGen provides no invariant constraints preventing one agent from overriding another agent's output.
AutoGen provides no write-scope quarantine governing which agents may emit side-effecting actions.
MetaGPT encodes standardized operating procedures into prompt sequences and assigns agents to specialized software-engineering roles.
MetaGPT's SOPs are task-workflow constraints rather than governance invariants.
MetaGPT does not define epistemic obligations, authority boundaries, or escalation gates for human principal approval.
LangGraph represents agent workflows as directed graphs with explicit state, conditional edges, persistent memory, and human-in-the-loop support.
LangGraph is relevant to Chirality's ORCHESTRATOR coordination layer as an orchestration substrate.
LangGraph provides no normative layer for impermissible state transitions, write authority, or evidence linkage to outputs.
Wang et al. provide a taxonomy of LLM-based autonomous agents organized around memory, planning, tools, and application domains.
The thesis uses Wang et al. as a reference taxonomy for classifying Chirality's architectural components against the literature.
Generative agents combine an LLM core with memory stream, reflection, and daily planning modules.
Generative-agent memory stores experience history as natural language, synthesizes reflections, and retrieves relevant context dynamically.
Generative agents demonstrate complex temporally extended behavior without hard-coded scripts.
Generative-agent societies do not address governance because agents lack shared-memory write constraints, authority hierarchy, and provenance records.
Constitutional AI reduces harmful outputs through a self-critique loop guided by a written natural-language constitution.
Constitutional AI trains models through reinforcement learning from AI feedback rather than human feedback for harmful-content labels.
Constitutional AI influenced Chirality's invariant-contract vocabulary as a constitutional layer specifying what agents must not do.
Constitutional AI applies principles at training time, whereas Chirality applies contracts at runtime as structural constraints on authority and epistemic obligations.
Hierarchical multi-agent frameworks use high-level agents to decompose tasks and delegate subtasks to specialized child agents.
Research cited in the thesis reports lower performance degradation for hierarchical topologies than decentralized structures under faulty-agent conditions.
Shavit et al. identify baseline governance obligations for agentic AI including minimal footprint, preference reversibility, and human check-in at task boundaries.
Hierarchical models establish the feasibility of tiered agent authority but do not formalize authority relationships as typed invariants.
Surveyed hierarchical frameworks do not enforce write-scope quarantine, gate-controlled authority escalation, or evidence structures for output claims.
The surveyed LLM agent literature optimizes for capability by defining and expanding what agents can do.
No surveyed architecture provides a formal governance layer specifying what agents must not do and what evidence they must provide.
Invariant contracts are absent from the surveyed literature as formally specified and runtime-enforced constraints independent of model weights or prompt content.
Write-scope quarantine is absent from the surveyed literature as an architectural boundary between read-only and write-capable operations.
Gate-controlled human authority is absent from the surveyed literature as a formal approval mechanism above defined authority thresholds.
Epistemic transparency obligations are absent from the surveyed literature as structural requirements for provenance, confidence class, and derivation path.
Chirality is designed to provide a governable agent system rather than merely a more capable agent system.
Section 2.2 surveys hallucination literature, trustworthiness frameworks, and mitigation approaches to motivate Chirality's per-claim transparency gap.
In natural language generation, hallucination means generated content that is unfaithful to a source document or unsupported by verifiable fact.
Ji et al. define hallucination along intrinsic and extrinsic axes.
Intrinsic hallucination contradicts source material, while extrinsic hallucination introduces information absent from the source.
Hallucination is treated in the thesis as a first-class reliability concern rather than an edge case.
Huang et al. distinguish factuality hallucination, unsupported by world knowledge, from faithfulness hallucination, inconsistent with provided context.
At the time described, all major commercial LLMs produced hallucinated content at measurable rates.
If hallucination is structural to current LLM generation, professional-engineering agent architectures must treat every model output as epistemically uncertain by default.
Maynez et al. found that all tested neural abstractive summarization models produced substantial hallucinated content.
ROUGE does not capture faithfulness, while textual entailment measures correlate more strongly with human faithfulness judgments.
Chirality requires provenance and grounding to be structurally explicit because output quality cannot be assessed from surface form alone.
FActScore decomposes long-form model generation into atomic facts and measures the proportion supported by a reliable external knowledge source.
In the cited evaluation, state-of-the-art commercial models supported only 58 percent of their atomic claims when independently verified.
The automated FActScore pipeline extracts, retrieves, and verifies claims with less than 2 percent error relative to human annotation.
FActScore verifies factuality after generation, whereas Chirality requires provenance attached at generation time as a structural obligation.
RLHF aligns LLM behavior through supervised fine-tuning, reward model training on human preferences, and PPO-based reinforcement learning.
The cited InstructGPT result shows that alignment quality is not determined by parameter count alone.
RLHF reduces expected hallucination rates at population level but provides no guarantee for individual outputs.
RLHF provides no runtime mechanism for a downstream system to determine whether a specific claim is grounded.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds generation in retrieved external documents rather than parametric memory alone.
Standard RAG does not enforce source citation in outputs.
Standard RAG does not distinguish directly retrieved claims from claims interpolated from model priors.
Standard RAG does not expose confidence or uncertainty metadata to downstream consumers.
Chirality's AUDITOR tier performs runtime architectural checks against invariant contracts with traceable audit output.
Modern neural networks can be poorly calibrated because predicted confidence scores do not match empirical accuracy rates.
Reliability diagrams and Expected Calibration Error diagnose calibration quality.
Temperature scaling is described as an effective single-parameter post-hoc calibration method.
Chirality assigns confidence class structurally based on claim derivation path rather than relying on model-reported confidence.

NIST AI RMF 1.0 defines trustworthy AI characteristics including validity, reliability, safety, security, resilience, accountability, transparency, explainability, interpretability, privacy enhancement, and fairness.
NIST AI RMF organizes AI risk management into Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions.
NIST AI RMF is a process framework and does not specify architectural mechanisms enforcing trustworthiness at system level.
Chirality is designed as a technical implementation of NIST trustworthiness characteristics for agentic systems in professional engineering practice.
The EU AI Act classifies AI systems by risk tier and imposes transparency and accountability obligations on high-risk systems.
Article 13 of the EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret outputs appropriately.
For multi-agent systems in professional engineering contexts, AI Act obligations apply to the system as a whole.
Chirality's invariant contracts, write-scope quarantine, and audit trail are designed as technical implementations of AI Act transparency and explainability obligations.
Training-time distribution shaping reduces expected hallucination rates by altering model priors but provides no per-output guarantee.
Post-hoc detection and evaluation measure hallucination rates after generation but are unavailable in real time at point of use.
Standard RAG is the closest existing approach to per-claim grounding but lacks enforced source attribution, typed uncertainty, and retrieved-versus-inferred distinctions.
Mandatory provenance attachment requires every system-output claim to carry a machine-readable pointer to its source observation or retrieved document.
The no-invention rule prohibits agents from generating claims that cannot be traced to a source within the defined retrieval scope.
Epistemic labelling distinguishes directly retrieved fact, inferred conclusion, and uncertain estimate as typed categories surfaced to the human principal.
Per-claim transparency makes the epistemic status of individual claims observable and auditable.
Chirality implements per-claim transparency as an architectural approach distinct from training-time and post-hoc population-level accuracy improvements.
Formal methods for safety-critical software provide rigorous techniques for specifying, verifying, and containing deterministic system behavior.
Formal methods require principled adaptation before application to governance of probabilistic LLM agents.
STAMP models complex sociotechnical failure as emergent behavior caused by inadequate constraint enforcement rather than linear causal chains.
STAMP treats safety as a control problem in which accidents occur when inadequate control actions violate safety constraints.
STPA derives safety constraints from control structure rather than failure mode enumeration.
Chirality's Runtime and Interaction Invariants can be read as STAMP-derived safety constraints applied to a software-agent control structure.
Chirality and STAMP both treat safety as an emergent property of constraint enforcement rather than component reliability.
DO-178C establishes five software levels based on failure-condition severity and defines objectives for the software assurance lifecycle.
DO-178C couples behavioral objectives to formal requirements traceability.
DO-178C requires every software behavior to be traceable to a verified requirement and every requirement to be satisfied by implementation.
DO-333 recognizes that proof-based verification can substitute for certain coverage-based testing objectives.
Chirality's lifecycle state machine constrains agent actions to defined phases with explicit transition conditions.
Chirality's Type 0, Type 1, and Type 2 hierarchy classifies agent authority by blast radius rather than failure severity.
IEC 61508 introduces Safety Integrity Levels SIL 1 through SIL 4, which quantify required reliability as a function of risk.
IEC 61508 mandates defense in depth through multiple independent protection layers.
IEC 61508 treats systematic failures as design-error failures rather than random hardware degradation.
IEC 61508 requires formal specification, systematic testing, and independent verification commensurate with assigned SIL for software safety.
Chirality maps independent protection layers to enforcement at instruction text, system prompt, agent runtime behavior, and human gate review.
Chirality's scope typing is structurally analogous to SIL assignment because constraint stringency is calibrated to consequence severity.
Rushby defines robust partitioning in integrated modular avionics through spatial and temporal separation requirements.
Fault containment is an architectural property that can hold when partition boundaries are correctly specified and enforced.
Containment infrastructure must be held to a higher assurance level than the functions it contains.
Chirality's write-scope system applies partitioning through Type 0 read-only, Type 1 project-scoped write, and Type 2 coordination-write agents.
Chirality enforces write-scope boundaries in the system prompt layer, isolated from the content layer the agent reasons about.
A Chirality agent cannot escape write scope through reasoning, analogous to a partitioned process being unable to access another partition's memory.
Hoare logic represents program verification through precondition, postcondition, and invariant triples.
Invariants are properties that hold across all states of a program loop or system lifecycle.
Model checking exhaustively explores reachable states and returns counterexamples when temporal-logic properties are violated.
TLA+ treats system behavior as a sequence of states and defines correctness as satisfaction of temporal-logic formulae over those sequences.
Chirality's lifecycle state machine is structurally a TLA+ specification even if not formally encoded as one.
Hoare logic, model checking, and TLA+ apply only partially to Chirality because LLM agents are probabilistic and lack enumerable internal state.
Chirality responds to unverifiable LLM behavior through invariant enforcement by external constraints rather than internal verification.
Hou et al. argue that trustworthy AI agents require integrating LLMs with formal methods because neither paradigm is sufficient alone.
The cited hybrid paradigm constrains agent behavior at the system boundary while LLMs operate within those constraints.
Freire et al. report that most formal verification techniques for safety-critical machine learning remain limited to small trained models under narrow assumptions.
Large Language Models present distinct formal-methods challenges because of scale, emergent behavior, and inability to be formally specified from first principles.
The governance-first paradigm argues that agent reliability requires principled governance infrastructure rather than behavioral training or post-hoc testing.
Chirality treats the agent instruction set as a governance constitution rather than a behavioral specification.
Classical formal methods assume the analyzed system has a specifiable state space and behavior formally related to requirements.
LLM-based agent systems violate deterministic verification assumptions because responses are probability distributions rather than functions.
LLM internal state is a high-dimensional embedding space that cannot be enumerated or formally analyzed.
Chirality adapts invariants, lifecycle state machines, write-scope containment, and precondition gates as external architectural constraints over non-deterministic agents.
The thesis frames the key shift as moving from algorithmic verification of deterministic systems to architectural governance of probabilistic agents.
Professional engineering regulation defines obligations of supervision, review, authentication, and accountability that predate AI systems.
Section 2.4 identifies the gap between regulatory obligations and AI-system architecture needed to enable compliance.
Chirality operates under Alberta jurisdiction, where APEGA licenses engineers under the Engineering and Geoscience Professions Act.
APEGA's Relying on the Work of Others and Outsourcing standard requires due diligence on reliability, accuracy, and validity of work performed by others.
APEGA's outsourcing standard requires confirming adherence to applicable regulatory requirements, standards, codes, and quality processes.
Failure to comply with APEGA's outsourcing standard is subject to disciplinary action.
AI agents in Chirality produce work that a licensed professional relies upon, making the APEGA outsourcing standard the primary regulatory instrument.
APEGA's outsourcing standard does not address how AI systems should be architected to enable required due diligence.
APEGA's Authenticating Professional Work Products standard defines authentication as the act by which a licensed professional accepts responsibility for a deliverable.
APEGA authentication requires a physical or digital stamp, APEGA member ID, and signature.
APEGA specifies that only work validated by the professional may be authenticated.
APEGA establishes the Notarius digital signature as the required mechanism for electronic authentication.
Chirality preserves authentication as an exclusively human gate action.
No Chirality agent has authority to authenticate a professional work product.
Chirality's lifecycle state machine holds deliverables in pre-authentication state until a human gate action advances them.
APEGA had not issued AI-specific guidance as of the thesis date, so general standards apply to AI outputs by direct interpretation.
The absence of APEGA AI-specific guidance is treated as an architectural gap addressed by the thesis.
EGBC released an AI professional-practice advisory on November 22, 2024.
EGBC states that engineering and geoscience professionals remain professionally responsible for work generated by or including AI output.
EGBC identifies AI-specific risks including output bias, automation bias, and context-dependent trustworthiness.
EGBC requires professionals using AI to assess their ability to meet checking, direct-supervision, document-retention, and independent-review requirements.
EGBC defines professional AI obligations but does not specify architectural requirements for AI systems.
Chirality addresses the EGBC architectural gap by using gate-controlled workflows that cannot be bypassed.
Professional Engineers Ontario had not issued its own AI-specific practice guideline as of the thesis date.
PEO references the EGBC AI practice advisory as a relevant resource.
PEO's absence of Ontario-specific AI guidance underscores the early state of regulatory development.
Engineers Canada had not issued a national AI guideline for professional practice as of the thesis date.
Absence of a national Engineers Canada AI guideline leaves provinces developing AI guidance independently.
Engineers Canada's AI position statement on autonomous vehicles addresses engineers as AI developers rather than AI-tool users.
NSPE states that individuals designing, developing, or overseeing safety-impacting AI systems should be held to professional licensure standards.
NSPE states that AI-generated technical work requires at least the same scrutiny as human-created work.
NSPE ethics guidance confirms licensed engineers cannot delegate professional judgment to AI systems and must exercise responsible charge over AI-assisted outputs.
ASCE states that AI cannot replace the professional judgment of a licensed Professional Engineer.
ASCE states that civil engineers must maintain responsibility for project planning, design, construction, operations, and maintenance.
ASCE acknowledges that rapid AI advancement is outstripping current laws and regulations.
ASCE Policy Statement 573 does not prescribe architectural requirements for AI systems.
FBPE guidance on AI-assisted work was not confirmed at the time of writing.

The cited risk-governance work finds that concrete accountability strategies for AI practitioners have not been adequately developed or communicated.
Responsible charge requires a licensed engineer to have actual knowledge of and responsibility for work done in their name.
AI system outputs that are not directly reviewed cannot satisfy responsible-charge requirements.
Chirality requires professional review to be structurally enforced rather than merely possible.
Across surveyed jurisdictions, licensed professionals using AI tools must review and validate AI-generated outputs before relying on them.
Across surveyed jurisdictions, licensed professionals cannot delegate professional judgment to AI systems.
Across surveyed jurisdictions, licensed professionals must be able to demonstrate that quality-control processes were followed.
Across surveyed jurisdictions, work products must be authenticated only after professional validation.
Across surveyed jurisdictions, professionals bear full liability for authenticated work products regardless of the generating tool.
Regulatory frameworks do not specify how AI systems should be architected to make professional obligations structurally satisfiable.

Chirality requires the epistemic status of every system-produced claim to be architecturally explicit and auditable.
Chirality treats epistemic status as an invariant enforced uniformly across agents rather than a quality aspiration or style guideline.
Section 2.5 identifies the gap that epistemic frameworks have been theorized but not operationalized as architectural invariants for LLM agent systems.
W3C PROV-DM provides a standardized framework for representing provenance information on the web.
PROV-DM defines provenance as information about entities, activities, and people involved in producing data or things for assessing quality, reliability, or trustworthiness.
PROV-DM organizes provenance into entities and activities, derivations, agents and responsibility, bundles, alternate entities, and collections.
PROV-DM is domain-agnostic and includes extensibility points for domain-specific information.
PROV-N provides human-readable PROV notation and PROV-O provides an OWL ontology serialization.
Chirality's K-PROV-1 requires every extracted or aggregated claim to carry a source file reference and section pointer or an explicit location TBD marker.
A Chirality provenance record consists of an entity, an activity, and an agent.
Chirality Dependencies.csv columns EvidenceFile, SourceRef, and EvidenceQuote implement the PROV-DM entity-activity-agent triad.
Chirality treats provenance as a structural invariant rather than optional metadata.
In Chirality, a claim without provenance is architecturally visible as ungrounded.
Database provenance distinguishes why-provenance from where-provenance.
Why-provenance identifies source tuples that contributed to an output tuple.
Where-provenance identifies the source database locations from which data values were copied.
Database provenance theory defines why, how, and where as orthogonal provenance axes.
Database provenance is established as a first-class semantic property of database systems rather than a secondary audit capability.
Chirality treats the presence of provenance as a structural requirement.
Chirality represents absence of provenance as the defined state location TBD rather than a null.
Chirality mirrors why-provenance in EvidenceQuote and where-provenance in SourceRef.
Chirality extends database query provenance to claim provenance in professional engineering deliverables produced by LLM agents.
Sowa's knowledge representation work bridges formal logic, ontology, linguistics, and computational implementation.
Knowledge representation determines what a system can reason about.
Expressive limitations of a representational system impose hard constraints on possible inferences.
Knowledge representations must be grounded in an underlying ontology.
The structure of an ontology shapes the inferences a system can support.
Representations lacking ontological discipline can produce formally valid but semantically empty inferences.
Chirality TYPES.md defines a canonical ontology of constructs that all agents are required to use.
Chirality epistemic labels restrict what inferences a licensed professional may draw without further validation.
Chirality encodes the justificatory status of claims as load-bearing metadata for subsequent reasoning.
The Bunge-Wand-Weber model applies Mario Bunge's ontology to information systems theory.
BWW core constructs include things, attributes, states, events, and couplings.
BWW defines representational, state-tracking, and good-decomposition models for information systems.
The extent of BWW secondary literature requires verification against Allen and March 2006.

UnitStatement: Chirality's K-HIER-1 and K-ID-1 invariants implement the BWW requirement that representational models contain no constructs without real-world referents.
In Chirality, every folder corresponds to a real work item and every dependency row corresponds to a real relationship.
In Chirality, every status file corresponds to a real lifecycle state.
Chirality permits no constructs for system convenience alone.
Chirality treats filesystem state as the authoritative project state.
In Chirality, divergence between filesystem state and actual project state is a governance failure rather than a mere data inconsistency.
Goldman's naturalistic epistemology holds that justification and knowledge must be evaluated by reference to the cognitive processes that produce beliefs.
Goldman's reliabilism treats a belief as justified when produced by reliable truth-conducive processes.
Goldman's veritistic social epistemology evaluates which social practices and institutions best foster true beliefs across a community.
Goldman's framework evaluates social systems as well as individual believers.
Well-designed institutions can substitute for individual epistemic competence when reliable individual judgment cannot be guaranteed.
In professional engineering practice, a licensed professional may be unable to personally verify every claim in a complex deliverable.
Chirality makes the reliability of the production process structurally visible to the professional.
Chirality's FACT label represents that a claim was produced by a reliable source-grounded process.
Chirality's ASSUMPTION label represents that a claim was produced by an inference process that may not be reliable for the asserted value.
Goldman's social epistemology grounds Chirality's K-CONFLICT-1 conflict surfacing mechanism.
Suppressing disagreement reduces collective epistemic performance by hiding information about epistemic uncertainty.
Chirality Conflict Tables require agents to surface disagreements, label proposed resolutions as PROPOSAL, and leave rulings to the human.
Silent conflict resolution by an agent violates the veritistic requirement by suppressing relevant epistemic information.
Halpern and Moses formalize processor knowledge states as sets of possible worlds consistent with local information.
Common knowledge is unattainable in practical distributed systems with communication delays.
Eventual common knowledge and epsilon-common knowledge are weaker knowledge variants attainable under realistic conditions.
Multiple-agent systems can contain agents with potentially inconsistent local knowledge states.
Distributed-system protocol design must account for inevitable divergent world views under communication delays or failures.
Chirality's conflict detection architecture treats agent divergence as expected rather than exceptional.
Chirality requires consensus to be detected, surfaced, and resolved rather than assumed.
Chirality Conflict Tables are epistemic reconciliation mechanisms implied by the Halpern-Moses framework.
Jacovi et al. distinguish intrinsic trust, extrinsic trust, and contractual trust in AI systems.
Contractual trust holds conditionally on an explicit or implicit contract being honored.
Designing AI systems for trust requires specifying the conditions under which the trust contract holds.
A trust claim about an AI system is meaningful only if observable conditions could falsify it.
Explanations and transparency mechanisms enable trust by making appropriate-trust conditions observable.
